newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN rights envoy says Iraq has "cruel dictatorship".
newsitem.headline: UN rights envoy says Iraq has "cruel dictatorship".

text.p: The U.N. special investigator for human rights in Iraq said on Friday that power remained in the hands of President Saddam Hussein's "cruel dictatorship" whose security apparatus freely killed and tortured opponents.

Former Dutch Foreign Minister Max van der Stoel, who serves as U.N. special rapporteur on Iraq, said in his annual report to the U.N. Human Rights Commission that there had been no improvement in the situation over the last year.
He also cited reports of thousands of arrests, "followed by many executions", related to the attempted assassination of Saddam's eldest son, Uday, last December.

Van der Stoel called on Baghdad to introduce democracy, abrogate all decrees which repress freedom of expression, bring its security forces under the rule of law and clear up the fate of 607 Kuwaitis and other nationals missing since the Gulf War.
He hoped that distribution of food and medical supplies under the U.N.'s oil-for-food deal with Iraq would be equitable.

The U.N. investigator was again denied access to Iraq, but based his report on information from sources including non-governmental organisations and staff of the U.N. Centre for Human Rights who had travelled to Jordan, Iran and Kuwait.

"The Special Rapporteur notes that, based upon the information in his possession, there has been essentially no improvement in the situation of human rights in Iraq," he wrote. "Fundamentally, all power is in the hands of a cruel dictatorship," he added.
"In short, Iraq is a dictatorial, totalitarian state which allows no political dissent. Freedoms of opinion, expression, association and assembly do not exist in Iraq."

Van der Stoel also condemned alleged executions and indiscriminate killings of civilians by Iraqi military and security forces in the north beginning in August 1996. He had received reports alleging that the Iraqi security services and their agents remained active in the northern Kurdish regions.
In addition, at least 30 military officers were said to have been executed at the end of June 1996 on suspicion of plotting to overthrow the regime, he said.
On repression after the attempt on the life of Uday, who survived the attack but still has bullets in his body, he said:

"Arrests and detentions without judicial orders are reported to have numbered in the thousands, cutting across all military forces and security services, the Baath Party, tribal leaders close to the President, and even extending to within the President's immediate family."
Mistreatment in detention, including beatings and other torture during interrogations, were said still to be widespread.

"Of vital importance to the maintenance of the present political regime in Iraq is the complex, vast and infamous security apparatus which the President controls directly and through his youngest son Qusay Hussein.
"The position of power enjoyed by the President is subject to the most extreme abuse which continues to bear especially heavily upon any threat of opposition -- real or perceived."
Impunity even for serious assaults and extrajudicial killings encouraged the abuse of power, he said.

"Such serious abuses of power over a period of decades, along with the effective proscription of dissenting opinion, expression, association or assembly, have acted to render Iraqis essentially compliant."
Iraq had decidedly the "worst record in the world" for the number of enforced or involuntary disappearances, as 16,199 cases remain unresolved over the years, van der Stoel said.
Some 607 Kuwaiti and other third-country nationals who went missing after being taken into custody by Iraqi forces during the 1990-91 occupation of the emirate are unaccounted for.

Iraq has supplied information on 128 cases to the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), but it has returned the remains of only two people since December 1994, according to the U.N. investigator.
